title: Survive a Market Crash

conceptsAssessed.concept: Reduce dependence on one company, sector, or outcome.
Separate sharp price movement from permanent failure or guaranteed recovery.
Use time as planning flexibility without assuming future growth.
Follow or adjust an affordable contribution plan through changing prices.
Review goals, investment quality, affordability, and emergency protection before reacting.

learningObjective: Apply volatility, diversification, regular investing, long-term planning, emergency-savings protection, and emotional control during a major market decline.
primaryMisconception: A major market decline means every investment has permanently failed and should be sold immediately.
secondaryMisconceptions: Market prices are guaranteed to recover after every decline.
Borrowing or using emergency savings is a good way to recover investment losses quickly.
Continuing regular investments during falling markets always guarantees a profit.
Diversification prevents all losses during a market crash.
keyTakeaway: Review the plan, protect emergency money, and do not confuse falling prices with guaranteed failure or recovery.

overview.summary: The learner manages a long-term portfolio after a sudden 25% decline. Five connected stages test the first reaction, social pressure, concentration risk, monthly contributions, and a five-year simulation with a genuine emergency. Sales, borrowing, emergency-fund use, diversification, and contribution choices persist into later stages. The final dashboard measures realised losses, portfolio value, contributions, emergency protection, debt, emotional decisions, diversification, long-term discipline, and financial confidence. The experience should feel tense but controlled, with replayable trade-offs and no guaranteed market outcome.

screens.title: Your Portfolio Just Fell
screens.content: Rs. 200,000 becomes Rs. 150,000 overnight. Headlines shout, friends panic, and your seven-year goal remains. What do you do first?
screens.illustration: A portfolio card drops beside urgent headlines and a seven-year calendar.

screens.title: The Starting Drop
screens.content: Your long-term portfolio has fallen 25%. The Rs. 50,000 decline is still unrealised because you have not sold.

screens.title: Money Outside the Market
screens.content: You have Rs. 30,000 general savings and a separate Rs. 100,000 emergency fund. Neither is part of the portfolio.
screens.illustration: Three separate containers for investments, cash, and emergency savings.

screens.title: Seven Years Still Remain
screens.content: The goal is at least seven years away. You also planned an affordable Rs. 10,000 monthly contribution.
screens.illustration: A seven-year timeline beside a monthly contribution card.

screens.title: What Should Come First?
screens.question: What should guide your first response to the 25% decline?

options.label: The loudest headline
options.feedback: Headlines cannot decide whether the portfolio still fits the goal.

options.label: A review of the goal, time horizon, and investment quality
options.feedback: Correct. Review creates space for evidence before fear or hope drives the decision.

options.label: A guarantee that prices will recover
options.feedback: No one can guarantee recovery.

options.label: Borrowing enough to replace the loss
options.feedback: Borrowing adds repayment pressure without reversing the existing decline.

screens.connectionToSimulation: The next five stages test review, social pressure, diversification, affordability, emergency protection, and uncertainty.

stages.title: First Market Drop
stages.situation: The portfolio has fallen from Rs. 200,000 to Rs. 150,000. The goal is still at least seven years away, but frightening headlines create pressure to act immediately.
stages.objective: Choose the first response and understand how it changes realised losses, debt, and later options.

educationalAssumptions: Borrowing Rs. 50,000 creates ten equal classroom repayments of Rs. 5,000.
No interest rate or fee is invented.
Selling at Rs. 150,000 realises the Rs. 50,000 decline.

choices.label: Sell everything immediately
choices.classificationReason: The sale happens before reviewing the goal or investment quality.
choices.immediateFinancialEffect: The portfolio is sold for Rs. 150,000.
choices.immediateFeedback: Selling removes future price uncertainty, but the Rs. 50,000 decline becomes realised.
choices.shortTermConsequence: Cash outside the portfolio becomes Rs. 180,000.
choices.laterConsequence: Later market paths affect only money invested again.

choices.label: Review the investment plan
choices.classificationReason: It separates evidence from immediate emotional pressure.
choices.immediateFeedback: Review the goal, time horizon, quality, fees, diversification, and need for the money.
choices.laterConsequence: Later choices can respond to evidence instead of fear alone.

choices.label: Borrow Rs. 50,000 to recover the loss
choices.classificationReason: Debt and market uncertainty are combined.
choices.immediateFinancialEffect: Debt and the portfolio each increase by Rs. 50,000.
choices.immediateFeedback: Borrowing does not recover the old loss. The new money may also fall.
choices.laterConsequence: Only Rs. 5,000 of the monthly contribution budget remains flexible in Stage 4.

choices.label: Ignore everything without checking
choices.classificationReason: Patience is used without reviewing whether the portfolio still fits.
choices.immediateFeedback: Avoiding panic can help, but long-term investing does not mean ignoring quality or suitability.
choices.laterConsequence: A concentration or quality problem may remain hidden.

recommendedDecisionLogic.strongestApproach: Review the goal, time horizon, diversification, fees, and investment quality before making a major change.
reasonableAlternatives: Selling may be reasonable after review if the investment is unsuitable or the money is needed sooner.
Remaining invested may be reasonable when the portfolio still fits, but only after review.
recommendedDecisionLogic.tradeOff: Selling removes future market exposure but realises the loss; staying invested preserves uncertainty and possible future movement.

validation.method: Accept one choice and apply all state changes.
validation.invalidStateFeedback: No choice is blocked. Review the trade-off before confirming.
validation.retryBehaviour: Risky choices may continue. The learner may revise once before the decision is carried forward.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Present four labelled buttons and a balance summary.
accessibilityAlternative.instruction: Choose one response and hear the investment, cash, debt, and loss changes.

stateSummary.title: First Response Recorded

changedValues.reason: Selling or borrowing changes market exposure.
A loss becomes realised only when sold below cost.

stateSummary.learningMessage: A price decline and permanent investment failure are not automatically the same.
stateSummary.nextStageTeaser: A friend now sends a confident prediction.

stages.title: Social Pressure
stages.situation: A friend says, “Sell now. The market will never recover. Everyone who waits will lose everything.” Your balances from Stage 1 remain in place.
stages.objective: Predict what the message can prove, then choose how to respond.

prediction.situation: A friend confidently predicts permanent market failure.
prediction.question: What does the message prove?

options.label: The market will never recover
options.feedback: A confident statement is not proof of a future result.

options.label: The friend is worried
options.feedback: Correct. The message reveals emotion and opinion, not certainty.

options.label: Every investment has failed
options.feedback: Different investments can have different problems and outcomes.

prediction.likelyEducationalOutcome: The learner separates social pressure from evidence.
prediction.explanation: Neither a friend nor the mission can know with certainty whether prices will recover.

choices.label: Follow the friend and sell
choices.classificationReason: The decision relies mainly on another person’s prediction.
choices.immediateFinancialEffect: Any remaining portfolio is sold at its current value.
choices.immediateFeedback: The sale removes future market exposure, but the decision is pressure-led.
choices.shortTermConsequence: The remaining portfolio moves to cash.
choices.laterConsequence: Later paths apply only to new contributions.

choices.label: Research the situation
choices.classificationReason: It checks causes and investment quality rather than one prediction.
choices.immediateFeedback: Review what caused the decline and whether the holdings remain suitable.
choices.laterConsequence: Stage 3 uses evidence instead of the friend’s claim.

choices.label: Review the original goal
choices.classificationReason: It checks whether the time horizon and strategy still fit.
choices.immediateFeedback: Compare the seven-year goal with the portfolio and current needs.
choices.laterConsequence: Contribution and emergency decisions stay linked to the goal.

choices.label: Assume recovery is guaranteed
choices.classificationReason: Hope replaces review and genuine problems may be missed.
choices.immediateFinancialEffect: The portfolio remains invested without review.
choices.immediateFeedback: Remaining invested may fit, but guaranteed recovery is not a valid reason.
choices.laterConsequence: A weak company or unsuitable portfolio may remain unaddressed.

recommendedDecisionLogic.strongestApproach: Research the decline and review the original goal before following anyone’s prediction.
reasonableAlternatives: Research and goal review are both strong and may be combined.
Selling may become reasonable after evidence shows the investment no longer fits.
recommendedDecisionLogic.tradeOff: Research takes time while uncertainty remains, but it reduces dependence on fear or guaranteed-recovery assumptions.

validation.method: Record the prediction, then one response.
validation.invalidStateFeedback: No response is blocked. Review whether it is based on evidence or prediction.
validation.retryBehaviour: The learner may revise before confirmation. The outcome then carries forward.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Use labelled prediction and response buttons.
accessibilityAlternative.instruction: Choose what the message proves, then choose how to respond.

stateSummary.title: Pressure Response Recorded

changedValues.reason: Selling turns an unrealised decline into a realised loss.

stateSummary.learningMessage: A confident prediction is not evidence of permanent failure or guaranteed recovery.
stateSummary.nextStageTeaser: Compare how concentration changes one company’s impact.

stages.title: Diversification Check
stages.situation: Two portfolios were each worth Rs. 200,000 before the decline. One depends on a single company. The other spreads money across companies, bonds, an ETF, and cash.
stages.objective: Compare the declines, identify concentration risk, and decide how to handle the learner’s own concentration.

learnerQuestions.question: Which portfolio depends more heavily on one outcome?
Which portfolio experiences the larger decline?
Did diversification prevent Portfolio B from losing money?

config.importantHiddenDifference: Portfolio A depends entirely on one company; Portfolio B spreads exposure across several investment types.
config.explanation: Diversification reduced dependence on one outcome in this illustration, but it did not prevent loss.
config.importantClarification: This is educational only. Diversification can reduce concentration risk but cannot guarantee smaller losses in every decline.

choices.label: Reduce concentration gradually
choices.classificationReason: The portfolio becomes less dependent on one outcome without assuming risk disappears.
choices.immediateFinancialEffect: No forced sale amount is applied; the plan is marked for gradual spreading.
choices.immediateFeedback: Dependence on one company or sector falls.
choices.laterConsequence: Weak simulated paths use the broadly spread setting.

choices.label: Keep the concentration after a full review
choices.classificationReason: The learner knowingly accepts higher concentration risk.
choices.immediateFeedback: The portfolio remains more dependent on one outcome.
choices.laterConsequence: Weak paths apply a larger concentration adjustment.

choices.label: Sell because diversification also lost money
choices.classificationReason: The choice treats risk reduction as failure because it did not remove all loss.
choices.immediateFeedback: Diversification does not promise zero loss.
choices.laterConsequence: Only new contributions enter later paths.

recommendedDecisionLogic.strongestApproach: Reduce extreme concentration when dependence on one outcome is high and the change fits the long-term plan.
reasonableAlternatives: Keeping concentration may be reasonable only after understanding the higher risk and ability to tolerate it.
recommendedDecisionLogic.tradeOff: More diversification reduces dependence on one outcome but cannot remove all market risk.

validation.method: Check all three comparison questions, then one concentration response.
validation.invalidStateFeedback: Review which portfolio depends on one company and whether Portfolio B still lost money.
validation.retryBehaviour: Keep correct answers and retry only incorrect comparisons. Risky portfolio choices may continue.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Present both portfolios as labelled tables with Previous and Next controls.
accessibilityAlternative.instruction: Compare values, answer three questions, then choose a concentration response.

stateSummary.title: Concentration Reviewed

changedValues.reason: The learner chose whether to reduce or keep dependence on one outcome.
Spreading exposure improves the score without guaranteeing protection.

stateSummary.learningMessage: Diversification reduces concentration risk; it does not prevent every loss.
stateSummary.nextStageTeaser: Decide whether the Rs. 10,000 monthly contribution still fits.

stages.title: Regular Contribution
stages.situation: You still have a Rs. 10,000 monthly contribution budget. Any debt repayment created earlier must come first, and emergency savings should remain separate from long-term investing.
stages.objective: Build a valid monthly plan and choose whether to continue, pause, misuse emergency money, or borrow.

scoringRules: Reward an affordable contribution or a clear pause reason.
Do not reward investing emergency money or borrowing.
validationRules: Required debt repayment must be covered.
Emergency withdrawals are outside the budget.

startingNode.question: How should the monthly plan respond to the decline?

educationalAssumptions: Investing emergency money uses Rs. 50,000 once.
Borrowing Rs. 50,000 creates ten classroom repayments of Rs. 5,000.
No interest rate or fee is invented.
Lower prices do not guarantee profit.

choices.label: Continue the affordable planned contribution
choices.classificationReason: The plan is affordable, emergency savings are protected, and required debt payments are covered.
choices.immediateFinancialEffect: The valid amount after debt repayment becomes the monthly contribution.
choices.immediateFeedback: Regular investing reduces dependence on one perfect entry point but does not guarantee profit.
choices.laterConsequence: Five-year totals use the confirmed amount.

choices.label: Pause contributions for a clear affordability reason
choices.classificationReason: Pausing may fit changed expenses, debt, emergency readiness, or goals.
choices.immediateFinancialEffect: No new money is invested this month.
choices.immediateFeedback: Pausing can be reasonable when circumstances changed; fear alone is weaker reasoning.
choices.shortTermConsequence: Unused money stays accessible after debt payments.

choices.label: Invest Rs. 50,000 of emergency money
choices.classificationReason: Emergency protection is exchanged for uncertain market exposure.
choices.immediateFinancialEffect: Emergency savings fall and the portfolio rises by Rs. 50,000.
choices.immediateFeedback: A later surprise may force debt or an investment sale.
choices.laterConsequence: The Year 2 emergency has fewer protected options.

choices.label: Borrow Rs. 50,000 to invest
choices.classificationReason: Repayment is certain while investment performance is uncertain.
choices.immediateFinancialEffect: Debt and the portfolio each rise by Rs. 50,000.
choices.immediateFeedback: Lower prices do not guarantee profit; the loan still requires repayment.
choices.shortTermConsequence: Monthly debt payments rise by Rs. 5,000.
choices.laterConsequence: The Year 2 emergency and contributions face more pressure.

recommendedDecisionLogic.strongestApproach: Continue an affordable contribution only after required repayments are covered and emergency savings remain protected.
reasonableAlternatives: Pausing is reasonable when income, expenses, debt, emergency readiness, or goals changed.
Continuing at a smaller amount is reasonable when debt repayment reduces the budget.
recommendedDecisionLogic.tradeOff: Continuing adds market exposure at several prices; pausing preserves cash but slows contributions.

validation.method: Validate the Rs. 10,000 budget and apply the selected decision.
validation.invalidStateFeedback: Cover required debt repayment and keep the total at exactly Rs. 10,000.
validation.retryBehaviour: Invalid budgets must be revised. Risky but valid emergency-fund and borrowing choices may continue.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Use plus and minus buttons followed by labelled decision options.
accessibilityAlternative.instruction: Build the Rs. 10,000 plan, then choose the contribution response.

stateSummary.title: Contribution Plan Updated

changedValues.reason: Debt repayment and affordability determine the contribution.
Emergency money changes only through top-up, genuine use, or misuse.

stateSummary.learningMessage: Regular investing should remain affordable and separate from emergency money.
stateSummary.nextStageTeaser: Explore three five-year paths and a real Year 2 emergency.

stages.title: Five-Year Uncertainty
stages.situation: Move through three possible five-year market paths. In Year 2, a genuine Rs. 40,000 household emergency occurs. All balances reflect earlier choices.
stages.objective: Separate contributions from market movement, handle the emergency, and finish with a reviewed—not guaranteed—long-term plan.

milestones.event: Portfolio is 25% below its original value.
A genuine Rs. 40,000 household emergency occurs.

timelineSlider.comparisonData: Each path uses the same learner decisions. Only fictional market movement changes.

Annual contributions equal the confirmed monthly amount multiplied by twelve.
Contributions are added after each year’s market movement for classroom simplicity.
No fees, taxes, dividends, or inflation are added.
A lucky path does not improve the decision score.

possibleFluctuations.label: Path A — Gradual Recovery
possibleFluctuations.explanation: The portfolio improves over several years, but this is only one possibility.

possibleFluctuations.label: Path B — Uneven Recovery
possibleFluctuations.explanation: The portfolio rises, falls again, and later stabilises unevenly.

possibleFluctuations.label: Path C — Continued Weakness
possibleFluctuations.explanation: Prices remain weak for years and some investments do not recover.

investmentSimulator.outcomeExplanation: Final value separates remaining opening balance, additional contributions, withdrawals, and fictional market movement.
investmentSimulator.requiredDisclaimer: These paths are fictional. Long-term investing provides more time for possible growth, but recovery, profit, and lower losses are not guaranteed.

prediction.question: After viewing all three paths, which conclusion is most accurate?

options.label: Waiting always restores every loss
options.feedback: Path C shows that weakness can continue and some investments may never recover.

options.label: Selling always prevents worse results
options.feedback: Selling may avoid later losses or miss later gains; review is still needed.

options.label: Several outcomes are possible, so the plan still needs review
options.feedback: Correct. Time helps planning, but it does not guarantee a result.

prediction.likelyEducationalOutcome: The learner accepts uncertainty without assuming guaranteed recovery.
prediction.explanation: Long-term investing still requires review of quality, goals, affordability, and risk.

choices.label: Use the emergency fund for the repair
choices.classificationReason: The money was kept accessible for genuine unexpected needs.
choices.immediateFinancialEffect: The emergency fund falls by Rs. 40,000.
choices.immediateFeedback: The repair is funded without a weak-market sale or new debt.
choices.laterConsequence: The investment plan can continue according to affordability.

choices.label: Use Rs. 30,000 cash and pause one Rs. 10,000 contribution
choices.classificationReason: Accessible money covers the emergency without debt when enough cash exists.
choices.immediateFinancialEffect: Cash falls and one contribution is redirected.
choices.immediateFeedback: The emergency is funded without debt.
choices.laterConsequence: The final investment value may be lower while emergency savings remain intact.

choices.label: Sell Rs. 40,000 of investments after review
choices.classificationReason: A reviewed sale may be necessary when accessible resources are insufficient.
choices.immediateFinancialEffect: Rs. 40,000 is withdrawn from the portfolio.
choices.immediateFeedback: The repair is funded, but part of the investment is sold during uncertainty.
choices.laterConsequence: Any loss on the sold portion becomes realised.

choices.label: Borrow Rs. 40,000 for the repair
choices.classificationReason: Debt adds pressure and may be avoidable if emergency savings were protected.
choices.immediateFeedback: Borrowing may be necessary when accessible money is insufficient.
choices.laterConsequence: Future contributions may need to fall.

recommendedDecisionLogic.strongestApproach: Use protected emergency savings for a genuine emergency when available, then rebuild them without assuming a market path.
reasonableAlternatives: Accessible cash plus a temporary contribution pause is reasonable when enough cash exists.
A reviewed sale or necessary borrowing may be required when protected resources are insufficient.
recommendedDecisionLogic.tradeOff: Protecting investments may reduce cash or emergency savings; protecting cash may require a sale, pause, or debt.

validation.method: Show all paths, check the uncertainty prediction, validate the emergency funding source, and calculate market outcome separately from the score.
validation.invalidStateFeedback: That funding source is insufficient for the Rs. 40,000 emergency.
validation.retryBehaviour: Insufficient choices must be revised. Risky feasible choices may continue. Replaying a path does not change the decision score.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Use Previous and Next buttons for years and paths, followed by labelled emergency choices.
accessibilityAlternative.instruction: Hear balances, contributions, losses, emergency savings, debt, and concentration at every point.

positiveDecisionFeedbackRules.message: You created space for evidence before making a permanent decision.
You did not treat another person’s prediction as certainty.

emergingRiskFeedbackRules.message: Investment debt is already reducing future flexibility.
The portfolio remains heavily dependent on one outcome.

midMissionCheckpoint.reflectionQuestion: Continue to the contribution decision, or review an earlier crash response?

finalChallenge.title: The Year 2 Emergency
finalChallenge.situation: During uncertain market conditions, an essential Rs. 40,000 household repair occurs. The strongest available choice depends on whether emergency savings, cash, investments, and debt were protected earlier.
finalChallenge.recommendedReasoning: Use protected emergency money when available. Otherwise compare accessible cash, a temporary contribution pause, a reviewed sale, and necessary borrowing without assuming recovery.

debrief.title: The Crash Did Not Decide Everything
debrief.content: You faced a sharp decline, confident predictions, concentration risk, a contribution decision, three possible market paths, and a genuine emergency. The fall did not prove permanent failure, but it also did not guarantee recovery. Reviewing the goal and investment quality separated evidence from fear or hope. Diversification reduced dependence on one outcome without preventing loss. Affordable regular contributions added money at several prices, while emergency savings and debt changed your flexibility. Selling, pausing, or remaining invested may each be reasonable after review. The strongest behaviour was not predicting the market—it was protecting essential money and making informed decisions.
debrief.simpleSummary: Review first, protect emergency money, and accept uncertainty without panic or guaranteed-recovery assumptions.
debrief.illustration: A market chart branches into three paths beside a review checklist, emergency shield, and debt meter.

dimensions.label: Emotional Decision-Making
positiveRules: 25 for evidence-based review and uncertainty awareness.
18 for mostly thoughtful choices with one emotional assumption.
8 for one panic sale or guaranteed-recovery assumption.
0 for repeated prediction-led decisions.
deductions: 8 for selling solely from a friend’s prediction.
10 for borrowing mainly to recover losses.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: Measures whether evidence, fear, hope, or social pressure guided the response.

dimensions.label: Diversification
positiveRules: 20 for correct comparisons and reducing extreme concentration.
14 for correct understanding while knowingly keeping concentration.
6 for expecting diversification to prevent every loss.
0 for ignoring concentration.
deductions: 5 for selling solely because the diversified example also declined.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: Measures understanding of concentration reduction without treating diversification as protection from all loss.

dimensions.label: Emergency Savings Protection
positiveRules: 20 for protecting emergency money until the genuine emergency.
16 for using accessible cash and a temporary pause.
8 for a necessary reviewed investment sale.
4 for necessary borrowing.
0 for emergency-fund investing followed by avoidable debt.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: Measures whether emergency money remained accessible for its intended purpose.

dimensions.label: Long-Term Discipline
positiveRules: 20 for reviewing and following an affordable plan.
16 for pausing or reducing for a clear reason.
8 for inconsistent decisions without emergency misuse.
0 for repeated borrowing, panic, or ignoring affordability.
deductions: 10 for abandoning the plan only because prices fell.
8 for ignoring the portfolio without review.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: Measures whether the long-term plan stayed affordable, reviewed, and adaptable.

dimensions.label: Financial Adaptability
positiveRules: 15 when later decisions fit actual cash, debt, emergency, and concentration state.
10 when one weak choice is corrected later.
5 when the plan works but creates avoidable pressure.
0 when later choices ignore the state created earlier.
deductions: 5 for an insufficient emergency funding source.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: Measures whether the plan changed thoughtfully as conditions changed.

questions.question: Which response combines volatility awareness and long-term planning?

options.label: Sell because the decline feels permanent
options.feedback: A feeling does not prove permanent failure.

options.label: Review the goal, portfolio quality, and need for the money
options.feedback: Correct. The choice uses both the price movement and the original plan.

options.label: Borrow because prices are lower
options.feedback: Lower prices do not guarantee profit while debt still requires repayment.

options.label: Assume every investment will recover
options.feedback: Some investments may remain weak or permanently lose value.

questions.correctExplanation: Reviewing connects volatility with quality, time horizon, and purpose.
questions.misconceptionTested: A major decline automatically proves permanent failure.

questions.question: A diversified portfolio falls during a crash. What does this prove?

options.label: Diversification failed completely
options.feedback: Diversification reduces dependence on one outcome; it does not promise zero loss.

options.label: The portfolio must recover
options.feedback: Recovery is possible but not guaranteed.

options.label: Diversification cannot remove all market risk
options.feedback: Correct. Several holdings may still decline together.

options.label: All holdings should be sold immediately

questions.correctExplanation: Diversification may reduce concentration risk while the portfolio still loses value.
questions.misconceptionTested: Diversification prevents all losses during a crash.

questions.question: A long-term investment falls 20%, and a medical bill is due. The person has emergency savings and no debt. What is the strongest first response?

options.label: Use emergency savings and review the investment separately

options.label: Invest the emergency savings at the lower price
options.feedback: This removes accessible money when a genuine emergency already exists.

options.label: Sell everything because the bill appeared
options.feedback: The investment can be reviewed separately when emergency money covers the bill.

realLifeChallenge.title: Write a Crash Checklist
realLifeChallenge.instruction: Write four questions you would ask before changing a fictional long-term investment after a price decline. Do not invest, sell, or share private financial information.

reviewChecklist.notes: Uses J4-M21, J4-M23, J4-M24, J4-M25, and J4-M26 concepts.

reviewChecklist.item: Does not introduce unexplained major concepts
reviewChecklist.notes: Realised loss, diversification, contributions, and emergency protection are explained in context.
Volatility, concentration, contributions, planning, and emergency savings affect one scenario.
The initial 25% decline equals Rs. 50,000; borrowing and emergency values reconcile.
Investments, cash, debt, losses, concentration, and emergency money carry forward.
Sales, borrowing, concentration, and emergency-fund use change later options.
Each major choice changes state, scoring, or later choices.

reviewChecklist.item: Multiple reasonable paths are allowed where appropriate
reviewChecklist.notes: Reviewed selling, pausing, continuing, cash use, and necessary borrowing may be defensible.
No recovery, profit, or loss-reduction guarantee is made.
Uses adult savings, debt, emergencies, and long-term goals.
Uses simple amounts, percentages, and direct consequences.
All holdings and paths are fictional educational examples.
Regular contributions and long-term investing remain uncertain.
The three paths are fictional simulations.

reviewChecklist.item: No claims that markets always recover
reviewChecklist.notes: The continued-weakness path directly rejects guaranteed recovery.

reviewChecklist.item: Simulated results are not presented as forecasts
reviewChecklist.notes: Decision quality is separate from fictional market paths.
Risky choices receive calm feedback.
Selling, pausing, borrowing, and staying invested are contextual.
Uses PKR, household emergencies, debt, and long-term planning.
All five stages apply crash-response skills.

reviewChecklist.item: Scoring rewards decision quality rather than luck
reviewChecklist.notes: The selected path cannot increase the decision score.

reviewChecklist.item: Enjoyable spending is not automatically treated as irresponsible
reviewChecklist.notes: The scenario focuses on investment and emergency decisions.
Borrowing and emergency-fund investing reduce the score.
The quiz addresses permanent failure, diversification, and emergency-money purpose.

reviewChecklist.item: Mission can be completed within the specified duration
reviewChecklist.notes: Five compact stages, a checkpoint, dashboard, and quiz fit nine minutes.

reviewChecklist.item: Language matches the target reading level
reviewChecklist.notes: Uses clear adult beginner language.
Every interaction includes labelled non-gesture controls.

reviewChecklist.item: Final dashboard matches the simulation outcomes
reviewChecklist.notes: Every dashboard item references tracked state or formulas.
Both artifacts are generated from the same mission data.
